title: Kindness
hookLine: the ninth perfection: goodwill to all
tomorrow: what do you say to the person who just hurt you?

lines: A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.
cards: A parent at the playground will hand out crackers to every kid in the sandbox, and still check on one of them every thirty seconds. That's how a parent's love works: fierce, and aimed at one. So here's the odd thing.

The Buddhist sutta on loving-kindness, the Karaniya Metta Sutta, reaches for exactly that picture. As a mother would protect her only child with her life, it says, so let a person grow a boundless heart toward all beings.
All beings. A love that picks one child out of the whole playground, used to describe a love with no favorites. Why?

teach.b: Look at what the sutta keeps, and what it drops. It keeps the strength. A mother who would protect her child with her life isn't making a polite wish; she'd step in front of a car.
And it drops the border. One child becomes all beings, and the sutta spells out who that means: weak or strong, large or small, seen or unseen, living near or far, born or still to be born.

Then it sends that goodwill out above, below and all around, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. That's the answer to the puzzle. The mother is the measure of the warmth, not of the circle.
The Pali word is metta: goodwill, friendliness, wishing beings well. And goodwill isn't the same as liking.
The same sutta sets a floor: let no one deceive another or despise anyone anywhere, or wish anyone harm in anger. You can find someone exhausting and still not wish them harm.
Buddhaghosa's meditation manual turns it into steps.

teach.h: STEP BY STEP, THE LINES BREAK DOWN.
teach.b: Begin with yourself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral, then someone hostile, and keep widening until the lines between them break down.
The sutta itself goes straight to the end: goodwill to all.

how: The Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted in Theravada communities as a protective chant, and metta meditation, wishing beings well in widening circles, is taught by Buddhist teachers today.

o: a calm, empty mind during meditation
a warm feeling for the people you like

games.q: what the sutta keeps and drops — tap the pairs.
p: despise no one, wish no one harm

s: metta means you have to like everyone
goodwill isn't liking. the sutta's floor: despise no one, wish no one harm.
the sutta compares goodwill to a mother protecting her only child
it keeps her strength and widens the circle to all beings.
the sutta's goodwill covers only the people you can see
seen or unseen, near or far, born or still to be born.

games.q: the neighbor's dog barks every night and you're running on no sleep. you're trying metta. what fits goodwill to all?
o: skip the neighbor for now. metta is for people you actually like.
wish the neighbor well, and still ask kindly about the barking.
never mention the dog. goodwill means never raising a problem.
games.why: goodwill isn't liking, and it isn't silence. the floor is wishing no one harm; you can do that and still ask about the dog.

practice: Close your eyes and wish one person well, plainly: may you be well, may you be safe. Then widen it, slowly, to everyone in your building, your street, your town, and out past where you can see.

wordCard.voice: Metta: goodwill, the wish that beings be well, with a mother's strength and no borders.

carryVoice: Your line: goodwill to all. The strength of one love, with the border taken off. Day twenty-five of thirty.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (also Khuddakapatha 9): as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so a boundless heart toward all beings; the list of beings; let none deceive or despise another
Visuddhimagga IX (the development of loving-kindness: oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person, then breaking down the barriers)
